title: KV eviction threshold slowdown retrospective
content:
Summary:

A staged rollout of a small change to the KV cache eviction heuristic (shard-level dynamic thresholding) caused an emergent P95/P99 latency increase for a subset of streaming inference sessions during the canary window on 2024-11-06. The change reduced per-shard cache residency for long-running streaming sessions that frequently extend sequence length and use prefix KV reuse. This produced a pattern of repeated KV cache misses and extra kernel work, amplifying tail latency for clients that maintain long-lived contexts.

Impact:
- 2024-11-06 03:40–04:30 UTC: Canary fleet (10% traffic) saw p95 latency increase from ~120ms to ~320ms and p99 went from ~300ms to ~2.1s for text-generation endpoints using model-v2.
- ~3% of overall customer requests during window experienced stalls or extra 500ms+ tail latency, concentrated in a small set of customers with long-session workflows (chatbot sessions > 2k tokens).
- No data integrity loss; responses were correct after delays. Some customers reported degraded UX for streaming completions.

Timeline (high level):
- 2024-11-05 20:00 UTC: Feature branch merged (dynamic-eviction-v2) — change enables shard-level eviction threshold to decrease linearly with measured per-shard active session count to free memory sooner on hotspots.
- 2024-11-06 01:10 UTC: Canary deploy started to canary fleet (10%). Basic metrics showed small mem savings.
- 2024-11-06 03:35 UTC: Pager fired (p95 latency) — SRE oncall alerted via synthetic monitors.
- 2024-11-06 03:37 UTC: Oncall joined Slack thread; initial hypothesis: abnormal batching/allocator pressure.
- 2024-11-06 03:45 UTC: Observed high KV miss rate and increased kernel allocation churn on canaries; rollback initiated.
- 2024-11-06 03:52 UTC: Canary rollback completed; metrics returned to baseline by ~04:15 UTC.
- 2024-11-07 10:00 UTC: Post-rollback debug session and deeper root cause analysis.

Detection and diagnostics notes:
- Alerts triggered by p95/p99 latency on the model-v2 route; synthetic session monitors for streaming endpoints were the first signal.
- Trace sampling revealed repeated KV load calls for the same session id across contiguous tokens where we expect hits. KV miss ratio on affected hosts rose from ~2% baseline to ~47% during the spike.
- Heap and GPU memory graphs showed no OOM but increased short-lived tensor allocations (quantization buffer rehydration) correlated with miss spikes.
- Canary-specific logs contained a new eviction-age calculation trace due to the dynamic threshold; using debug-level traces we saw that active-session heuristic decreased the eviction threshold aggressively when session count climbed beyond 40 per shard.
- A small segment of customer traffic uses very long sequences (chat histories with >2k tokens). These sessions repeatedly relied on prefix KV hits to avoid recomputing attention caches. Under the new heuristic those prefixes were evicted earlier than before, causing recomputation.

Root cause analysis (summary):
- The dynamic shrink of per-shard eviction threshold was tuned to free memory for hotspots but did not account for long-tail session length distributions.
- The heuristic used a linear factor that overreacted to short spikes in active-session counts (e.g., bursty reconnects) and did not weight by average sequence length or reuse ratio.
- Result: frequently-reused KV entries were evicted during the same logical session, forcing rehydration and extra kernel work that amplified tail latency.
- Secondary contributor: an optimization in the quantization pipeline altered buffer reuse timing for rehydrated caches, increasing short-lived allocations; combined with eviction churn this caused brief scheduler stalls and extra memcpy operations.

Why this wasn't caught in testing:
- Unit and integration tests covered eviction correctness but not the interaction between eviction heuristics and long-lived streaming sessions at scale.
- Canary traffic mix is usually representative, but this canary window coincided with an unusual mix of a few customers running long interactive sessions (low-probability but high-impact). Load testing harness simulates average session lengths and did not include long-tail session replay.

Mitigation and rollback steps taken:
- Immediate rollback of dynamic-eviction-v2 from canary fleet (03:45–03:52 UTC).
- Re-enabled previous conservative eviction thresholds across fleets.
- Flushed intermediate debug-level traces and captured representative KV miss traces from affected sessions for offline analysis.
- Notified affected customers in thread for transparency and offered elevated support for any follow-ups.

Longer-term remediation actions (action items):
1) Rework eviction heuristic: include weighted factors for average sequence length and KV reuse ratio; make threshold change rate-limited and add a cooldown window for shards with high reuse scores. (Owner: Alex Rivera, ETA: 2024-11-20)
2) Add regression tests that replay long-session traces against new eviction policies and measure KV hit-rate and p95 latency; include stochastic add-on tests that inject bursty reconnects. (Owner: Priya Narang, ETA: 2024-11-14)
3) Adjust canary rollout policy to include synthetic long-session traffic (configurable per model route) and make the canary stop criteria include KV miss-rate delta > 10%. (Owner: SRE platform, ETA: 2024-11-12)
4) Revisit quantization buffer reuse timing to ensure rehydration path is amortized; reduce short-lived tensor churn by preallocating reuse pools for rehydration hot paths. (Owner: serving-runtime, ETA: 2024-12-01)
5) Instrument additional metrics: per-shard reuse-score, sequence-length histogram, KV eviction/reinsertion latency, and per-session recompute count. Expose these in the console and add alerts. (Owner: observability team, ETA: 2024-11-18)
6) Update rollout checklist: require explicit verification of reuse-sensitive metrics when changing cache or memory heuristics. (Owner: release-eng, ETA: 2024-11-10)

Runbook / Oncall playbook updates (immediate):
- New runbook entry: "KV eviction-induced latency" under SRE playbooks. Steps: check per-shard KV hit-rate, sequence-length histograms, dynamic-threshold traces; if miss-rate delta > 20% and p95 > baseline +150ms, contact serving-runtime oncall and roll back.
- Add quick synthetic test to oncall tools that opens a 2500+ token streaming session and measures p95; run during canary verification.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- What other heuristics (beyond session count) should influence eviction? (reuse ratio, average token length, request frequency, user priority)
- Should we allow customers to set "pinned KV" annotations for known long-lived sessions (e.g., enterprise chatbots) to avoid eviction? Pros/cons from resource fairness perspective.
- Evaluate cost tradeoff: retaining more KV for reuse vs increased memory footprint and potential fragmentation.

Communications and customer impact notes:
- We proactively messaged affected customers within 2 hours of detection; no PII exposed, no dropped completions.
- Internal blameless postmortem shared with product and customer success; SRE lead presented a 15-minute summary in the daily ops sync (2024-11-07).

Appendix: useful traces and snippets (excerpts)
- Sample trace 1: repeated KV get miss for session_id=abc123 at token offsets 1024, 1025, 1026 despite expected hits. (attached in PR link above)
- Eviction decision log excerpt: "shard=7 active_sessions=46 avg_len=742 reuse_score=0.21 threshold=0.12 -> evict oldest entries"
- Kernel churn correlating chart: short-lived allocation rate x10 in the 7 minute window that aligns with KV miss spike.

Owner notes / retrospective thoughts:
I underestimated the coupling between a memory-first eviction strategy and the tail behavior of streaming workloads. We prioritized memory stabilization for hotspot shards but did not surface the reuse signal into the heuristic. The rollback was quick and effective; we should harden canary test coverage for long-tail sessions and incorporate reuse-aware signals before any future eviction policy changes.

Document history: created by Maya Chen (oncall) 2024-11-07; reviewed and edited by Alex Rivera, Priya Narang, Samir Patel, Jess Li; final version 2024-11-09.
